sections.label: Protection from Harassment Act history
sections.summary: The Protection from Harassment Bill was debated in 2014, and the Act was amended in 2019 to cover online harassment.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: As far back as 2014, when the Protection from Harassment Bill was debated, Ms Tin Pei Ling asked about removing offensive content and identifying perpetrators online.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: In 2019, we amended the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) to cover online harassment.

sections.label: SHE online harm studies
sections.summary: SHE studies found two in five survivors experienced severe impact and three in four victims stay silent online for fear of targeting.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: Subsequent studies by SHE showed that two in five online harm survivors experienced at least one severe form of impact.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: Three in four victims of online harms choose not to voice their opinions online for fear of being targeted if they did so.

sections.label: MDDI harmful content study
sections.summary: An MDDI study found more than four in five had encountered harmful online content in the past year.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: A Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) study revealed that more than four in five had encountered harmful online content in the past year.

sections.label: IMDA platform response study
sections.summary: An IMDA study showed platforms take about five days or more to act on valid reports of online harms.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: A study by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) showed that platforms take about five days or more to act on valid reports of online harms.

sections.label: New online harms legislation
sections.summary: Legislation is being introduced to give victims of online harms timely, effective and accessible redress.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: Today, we are taking a decisive step to introduce legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: It will give victims of online harms an avenue of timely, effective and accessible redress.

sections.label: OSRA thirteen harm types
sections.summary: OSRA identifies thirteen types of harms affecting Singaporeans from all walks of life.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: OSRA identifies thirteen types of harms which affect Singaporeans from all walks of life.

sections.label: Online Safety Bill three areas
sections.summary: The Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill focuses on three main areas, and establishing the OSC will let victims receive help more quickly.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: The Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill focuses on three main areas to strengthen online safety and protect Singaporeans from online harm.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: First, establishing the OSC will enable victims to receive help more quickly.

sections.label: Unlawful online behaviour and civil action
sections.summary: The Bill lists unlawful online behaviour, allowing victims to take civil action and making perpetrators bear legal consequences.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: Second, the Bill also clearly lists out unlawful online behaviour, allowing victims to take civil action against the perpetrators and make perpetrators bear legal consequences for their actions.

sections.label: Age assurance on app stores
sections.summary: Age assurance measures have been introduced on app stores to moderate such risks.

sentences.speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
sentences.text: To moderate such risks, we have introduced age assurance measures on app stores.

sections.label: Thirteen categories of harm
sections.summary: Part 3 of the Bill will specify 13 categories of harm, each defined in legislation, to create a common understanding of scope and definition.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Part 3 of the Bill will specify 13 categories of harm, with each category defined in legislation, to create a common understanding of the scope and definition of each type of harm.

sections.label: Definition of online harassment
sections.summary: Online harassment is defined as communicating online material a reasonable person would conclude is threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent and likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Online harassment is defined as the communication of online material that a reasonable person would conclude is threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent, and is likely to cause a person harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

sections.label: Intimate image abuse harm
sections.summary: Intimate image abuse, or the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, is a harm that can severely and lastingly impact victims.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: Fourth, intimate image abuse or the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, a harm that can result in a severe and lasting impact on victims.

sections.label: Online instigation of disproportionate harm
sections.summary: The eighth category of harm covers online instigation of disproportionate harm, addressing mob behaviour or cancel campaigns.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: The eighth category is online instigation of disproportionate harm.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: This harm seeks to address the issue of "mob behaviour" or cancel campaigns, where one individual calls for numerous others to pile on to another person, in response to the person's actions or speech, instigating disproportionate harm.

sections.label: Excluded harms and existing measures
sections.summary: Sexual grooming and online material promoting suicide or self-injury were not included as they are addressed by the Penal Code and Broadcasting Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: These two categories of harm differ slightly from the others in terms of the remedies victims may seek.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: There have been suggestions to include two new categories, namely sexual grooming and the publication of online material that encourages or promotes suicide or acts of self-injury.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: These harms have not been included at this stage, because, firstly, these harms are already addressed through other measures in our broader online safety framework, through the Penal Code for sexual grooming, and the Broadcasting Act for online material that encourages or promotes suicide or acts of self-injury.

sections.label: OSRA complements existing legislation
sections.summary: OSRA complements existing legislation by expanding covered harms and letting victims seek simple, timely recourse, as cost deters legal action.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: However, victims have shared that seeking legal remedies is often a lengthy and expensive legal process, which often deters them from seeking recourse.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: This can be seen from the SHE's 2023 Online Harms Report, which showed that 28% of respondents who decided not to take legal action did so due to the cost.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: OSRA is intended to complement these existing legislations by expanding the scope of harms covered, through including new harms, such as inauthentic material abuse and non-consensual disclosure of private information, and by allowing victims to seek recourse in a simple and timely manner.

sections.label: Commissioner delegation and OSC setup
sections.summary: The Commissioner may delegate functions to OSC officers except appointment, delegation and advisory guidelines, with the OSC to be set up in 2026.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: The Commissioner may delegate the exercise of all of, or any of, the functions or powers of the Commissioner to the officers of the OSC, to allow them to effectively support the Commissioner.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: This includes the power to issue directions, which I will speak more on later.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: However, the Commissioner may not delegate the power of appointment or delegation, or the power to issue advisory guidelines.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: As announced by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong during his speech at the Smart Nation 2.0 Launch in October 2024 and reiterated by Minister Josephine Teo earlier in March this year, the OSC will be set up in the first half of 2026.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
sentences.text: To that end, the Commissioner will consider publishing regular reports for public awareness on online harms and the Commissioner's work, which may include information on aggregated caseloads, and anonymised information, insofar as these do not re-traumatise victims.

sections.label: Reporting to platforms before OSC
sections.summary: Victims can report to OSC after platforms fail to act within 24 hours, but this is not required for egregious harms.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Where platforms fail to act on online harms within 24 hours, victims can then file a report to OSC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: The requirement to first report to platforms before reporting to the OSC will, however, not be required for certain egregious harms, such as intimate image abuse and image-based child abuse.

sections.label: Eligibility to submit a report
sections.summary: Victims must be Singaporean Citizens, Permanent Residents or have a prescribed connection to Singapore to submit a report.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: To be eligible to submit a report, victims must be Singaporean Citizens, Permanent Residents or have a prescribed connection to Singapore.

sections.label: Threshold for issuing directions
sections.summary: The threshold for issuing directions was set at "reason to suspect" rather than "reasonable grounds to believe" to stop online harms in a timely manner.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: We had considered raising the threshold for the issuance of directions to "reasonable grounds to believe".

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: However, we ultimately landed on "reason to suspect", to ensure that online harms can be stopped in a timely manner.

sections.label: Penalties for non-compliance with directions
sections.summary: Non-compliance with directions carries fines or imprisonment for individuals and larger fines for entities, with continuing fines after conviction.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: For example, the penalty for non-compliance with directions will be a fine of up to $20,000, or imprisonment for a period not exceeding 12 months, or both, for individuals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Individuals will also be subject to a continuing fine of up to $2,000 for each day the offence continues after conviction.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Entities will be subject to a fine of up to $500,000 and a continuing fine of up to $50,000 for each day the offence continues after conviction.

sections.label: Two-step appeal process
sections.summary: Victims, recipients of directions or orders, and other prescribed persons have a two-step appeal process, ending at an independent appeal panel appointed by the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Victims, recipients of directions or orders, and other prescribed persons will have access to a two-step appeal process.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: Thereafter, eligible persons may appeal against the OSC's reconsidered decision to an independent appeal panel that will be appointed by the Minister for Digital Development and Information.

sections.label: Composition and focus of appeal panel
sections.summary: The appeal panel consists of individuals from academia, society and industry and assesses whether a specified online harm occurred and whether the OSC's reconsidered decision is proportionate and justifiable.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: The appeal panel will consist of individuals from academia, society and industry, across different areas of expertise, and will focus on assessing whether a specified online harm had occurred and whether the reconsidered decision made by the OSC is proportionate and justifiable.

sections.label: First five harms in force
sections.summary: The first five harms will be brought into force within the first six months after the OSC opens, including intimate image abuse, image-based child abuse, and online harassment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: What this means is that we will be bringing the first five harms I shared about earlier into force within the first six months after the OSC opens its doors.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
sentences.text: These are: intimate image abuse; image-based child abuse; online harassment, including sexual harassment, doxxing and online stalking.

sections.label: Bill duties and Statutory Torts Framework
sections.summary: The Bill clarifies duties, provides relief and strengthens accountability across the online ecosystem, and the speaker focuses on the Statutory Torts Framework and End-User Identification measures.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The Bill before this House clarifies duties, provides relief and also strengthens accountability across the online ecosystem to deal with online harms.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: My colleagues have earlier taken Members through the key aspects of the Bill, and I will focus on outlining the new Statutory Torts Framework, as well as the End-User Identification measures in this Bill.

sections.label: Girl's online harm and PTSD
sections.summary: A girl received hurtful messages and comments about her appearance, self-harmed, and was later diagnosed with PTSD after seeking help at IMH.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: She began receiving comments about her appearance and hurtful messages from those who were supposedly her friends.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: She self-harmed and she was later diagnosed with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) when she eventually sought help at the Institute of Mental Health (IMH).

sections.label: SHE 2023 online harms findings
sections.summary: The SHE 2023 Study found 76% of respondents uncomfortable expressing controversial views online, with women, youths and minorities especially vulnerable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In the SHE 2023 Study on Online Harms cited by Minister of State Rahayu a short while ago, 76% of respondents were not comfortable expressing their personal views on potentially controversial issues and topics online.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Women, youths and minorities are especially vulnerable: 22% of female youths experienced sexual harassment compared to 14% across all respondents; 52% of respondents aged 15 to 24 years old personally experienced online harms compared to 38% across all respondents; 14% to 21% of respondents believed they experienced harms because of their identity, such as race and religion.

sections.label: SHE 2023 online harms experience
sections.summary: The SHE 2023 study found 58% of respondents reported personally experiencing and/or knowing others who faced online harms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The SHE 2023 study found that 58% of respondents reported personally experiencing and/or knowing others who faced online harms.

sections.label: IMDA study on unaddressed complaints
sections.summary: In the IMDA study cited by Minister Josephine Teo, over 50% of legitimate user complaints were not addressed in the first instance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Indeed, in the IMDA study cited by Minister Josephine Teo a short while ago, over 50% of legitimate user complaints were not addressed in the first instance.

sections.label: Clauses 83 to 88 harmful activities
sections.summary: Clauses 83 to 88 cover intimate image abuse, image-based child abuse, online impersonation, inauthentic material abuse, online instigation of disproportionate harm, and incitement of violence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Clauses 83 to 88 cover the following harmful online activities: intimate image abuse; image-based child abuse; online impersonation; inauthentic material abuse; online instigation of disproportionate harm; and incitement of violence.

sections.label: Duties on communicators
sections.summary: Clauses 83 to 88 impose duties on communicators not to make or share online harms, including not developing or maintaining online locations facilitating such harm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Clauses 83 to 88 therefore impose duties on communicators not to make or share any communication which constitutes an online harm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: First, they must not develop or maintain an online location in any manner that facilitates or permits online harm to take place – with the intention or knowledge that online harm is likely to take place.

sections.label: Platform duty when notified
sections.summary: Clause 94 imposes a similar duty on platforms to act reasonably when notified of harm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Clause 94 therefore imposes a similar duty on platforms to act reasonably when notified of harm.

sections.label: Victim damages under clause 96
sections.summary: Clause 96 lets victims seek damages the Court finds just and equitable, plus other damages the Minister may prescribe.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Under clause 96, victims may seek damages that the Court finds just and equitable, and other heads of damages that the Minister may prescribe in regulations, such as compensation for loss of earnings or an account of profits where perpetrators benefited from the harm.

sections.label: Enhanced damages for persistent conduct
sections.summary: Clause 98 introduces enhanced damages, empowering the Court to award them where a communicator or administrator persists despite notice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Clause 98 introduces the concept of enhanced damages and empowers the Court to award such damages where a communicator or administrator persists with their conduct despite notice.

sections.label: Court injunctions and independence
sections.summary: Clause 99 empowers the Court to issue interim and permanent injunctions, and the OSC and Courts are independent of each other.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In addition, clause 99 empowers the Court to issue injunctions, both interim as well as permanent, to stop harm swiftly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The OSC and the Courts operate independently of each other, and neither is bound by the decision of each other.

sections.label: End-User Identification measures option
sections.summary: Victims still need Court proceedings, which may be costly and time-consuming, so the Bill's End-User Identification measures offer an accessible option.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But victims will still need to commence Court proceedings which may be costly and time-consuming.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And so, we believe the Bill's proposed End-User Identification measures offer an accessible option.

sections.label: OSC user identification powers
sections.summary: Clause 52 empowers the OSC, on reasonable suspicion of online harm, to require prescribed platforms to obtain information identifying the user.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Second, clause 52 empowers the OSC, where it reasonably suspects a user of committing an online harm, to require prescribed platforms to take reasonable steps to obtain specified information that may identify the user.

sections.label: OSC disclosing perpetrator identity to victims
sections.summary: Clause 53 lets the OSC disclose a perpetrator's identity information to a victim or their authorised representatives upon the victim's application.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Third, clause 53 empowers the OSC to disclose the perpetrator's identity information to a victim or to their authorised representatives, upon receiving an application from the said victim.

sections.label: OSC conditions on information use
sections.summary: The OSC may impose strict conditions on information use, such as limiting it to seeking protection or pursuing legal remedies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: First, the OSC may impose strict conditions on how the information can be used, such as limiting the use of the information to seeking protection or pursuing legal remedies.

sections.label: OSC administrative decisions and judicial review
sections.summary: The OSC makes administrative decisions assessing harm using prescribed factors and public interest, subject to judicial review and not appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In the first place, the framework that you heard Minister of State Rahayu outline earlier, these are administrative decisions by the OSC, who assess the harm based on the prescribed factors in this framework and they make a poly-centric decision, taking into account policy and public interest considerations when deciding on whether it is a harm and if so, what the appropriate remedy ought to be.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: Such administrative decisions are subject to judicial review and not an appeal.

sections.label: Public consultation support for online harms measures
sections.summary: The 2024 MinLaw and MDDI public consultation showed over 90% support for a dedicated agency, over 95% for legal action, and over 80% for disclosure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In the Public Consultation launched by MinLaw and MDDI in 2024, respondents expressed strong support for establishing a dedicated agency to address online harms – over 90% support; allowing victims to take legal action, such as seeking compensation in Court for private remedies on top of the OSC framework – over 95%; disclosing a perpetrator's user information to the victim for certain specified purposes – over 80%.

sections.label: Engagements with technology companies
sections.summary: Over 20 engagement sessions with technology companies in the past two years aimed to ensure the Bill's provisions are robust, workable and feasible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We learnt much from their experiences and their insights and their stories.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: We also conducted over 20 engagement sessions with technology companies in the past two years to ensure that the provisions in the Bill are robust, workable, feasible and can be carried out when OSC issues directions.

sections.label: Steering Committee, symposium and public input
sections.summary: A Steering Committee, an SMU symposium, SHE's surveys and SHECARES@SCWO, and public consultation responses informed the policy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: As mentioned by Minister of State Rahayu, we convened a Steering Committee who guided our team in shaping our policy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: In addition, SMU Yong Pung How School of Law partnered us to organise our Online Harms Symposium.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The sharing from the experts and survivors at the Symposium informed much of our thinking on this matter.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: SHE's surveys and research on online harms and their experience in running SHECARES@SCWO, Singapore's first support centre for targets of online harms, provided us with data and insights to refine our policy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: And, finally, all those, many from the public who responded to our public consultation or who have engaged with us with very constructive comments and suggestions or written to my Ministry to share their stories.

sections.label: Residents encountering harmful online content
sections.summary: Surveys show over 84% of residents have encountered harmful online content and about one in three faced harassment or bullying.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: Surveys show that more than 84% of residents have encountered harmful content online and roughly one in three have faced harassment or bullying.

sections.label: Slow Court removal processes
sections.summary: Removal through current Court processes can take months or years, and traces often persist after takedown.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: Yet removal through current Court processes can take months and even years and traces often persist after takedown.

sections.label: Digital commons and timely justice
sections.summary: It gives people, especially youths, room to think and disagree, and lets OSC act in days to remove content, restrict accounts and disclose identities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: It gives our people, especially our youths, room to think and disagree without destruction – a healthy digital commons to engage, create, and learn without humiliation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: It delivers timely justice because harm spreads fast and hours matter, and OSC can act in days to remove content, restrict accounts and disclose identities so victims can seek damages.

sections.label: Evidentiary threshold in amendments
sections.summary: The amendments move the evidentiary threshold from "reason to suspect" to "reasonable grounds to believe".

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: In the amendments put forward, the evidentiary threshold moves from "reason to suspect" to "reasonable grounds to believe".

sections.label: MDDI and SHE online harms surveys
sections.summary: An MDDI survey found four in five respondents encountered harmful online content, and SHE's survey found one in two respondents aged 15 to 24 reported being victims.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: A survey released by MDDI last month found that four in five respondents have encountered harmful online content.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In May and June 2023, SHE's survey on online harms found that one in two respondents aged between 15 and 24 reported having been victims of online harms.

sections.label: Bill excludes suicide and self-harm material
sections.summary: The Bill does not include the publication of online material, encouraging or promoting suicide or self-harm.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Yet, the Bill before us does not include the publication of online material, encouraging or promoting suicide or self-harm.

sections.label: Harmful sexual content and grooming
sections.summary: An MDDI survey found 26% encountered harmful sexual content, and sexual grooming risks appear not explicitly covered by the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: An MDDI survey also noted that 26% of the respondents reported that they have encountered harmful content of a sexual nature.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Thus, with easy access to posts and content online, the high risks of sexual grooming of our minors and vulnerable adults are also of grave concern, but do not appear to be explicitly covered by the provisions of this Bill.

sections.label: Grooming excluded from OCHA
sections.summary: Excluding sexual grooming of minors and vulnerable adults from the Bill misses protections such as takedown orders.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Additionally, publication or communication of such online content, which may be directed at certain groups of persons, not just an individual, would appear not to be covered by the OCHA.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Thus, by excluding sexual grooming of minors or vulnerable adults under this Bill, we miss out an important protection of our children and vulnerable adults in the form of, for example, allowing takedown orders to be made.

sections.label: Victims reliving trauma in processes
sections.summary: Parallel processes force victims to relive experiences, backed by a SHE survey on emotional and mental health impact.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: If there are any parallel processes, such as actions taken out of statutory torts or Penal Code offences, the victim would often have to relive and recount their experiences, the impact it has had on them and if there is a trial, subject to cross examination of the extremely traumatic event or events.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is backed up by a SHE survey, which found that two in five victims of online harm experienced serious emotional or mental health impact, such as depression or fear for safety.

sections.label: Costs of filing civil claims
sections.summary: Statutory torts are welcome, but civil claims require victims to gather evidence, bear costs and relive harms.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The inclusion of these statutory torts is welcome and empowering, but we must not forget that to file a civil claim, victims must gather evidence, bear legal costs and relive the harms done to them time and again.

sections.label: Specialists for new agency
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the new agency will have trauma-informed specialists, gender-based violence experts and experienced lawyers.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Will the new agency have specialists, such as psychologists who understand trauma-informed approaches, gender-based violence experts, lawyers experienced in not just defamation and harassment law, but who also understand the often insidious and subtle means in which perpetrators of online harms attempt to assert power and coercive control over their targets, sometimes in the context of post-separation abuse.

sections.label: Amendments on fair comment appeals
sections.summary: Amendments to clauses 9, 11, 19 and 26 cover fair comment, and new clause C allows appeals to the judicial system.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As such, we have tabled amendments to clauses 9, 11, 19 and 26, to ensure that individuals can communicate online material that constitutes fair comment on matters of public interest.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: To further strengthen our understanding and faith in the regime, we have also included new clause C, allowing appeals to the judicial system.

sections.label: Commissioner annual report amendments
sections.summary: Amendments require the Commissioner to submit an annual report to Parliament and to require online service providers to disclose their measures against online harms.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The final group of amendments that we have tabled call for the Commissioner to prepare and submit an annual report to Parliament and specify the areas which should be covered by the report.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The proposed new clause E also gives the Commissioner explicit powers to require online service providers to disclose information about their own measures to tackle online harms.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Such information is particularly necessary in line with the Institute of Policy Studies' findings that 75% think that, apart from Government and users, tech companies also must do more to tackle online harms and that the 2024 MDDI survey found that 80% of respondents who reported online harms experience issues with platforms reporting processes.

sections.label: Duty to remedy harms
sections.summary: The duty to remedy harms is complicated and the balance sought will be tested, but the proposed amendments allow better legislation.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Our duty to remedy harms is highly complicated and the balance that we seek in legislation and practice will be tested by edge cases, unforeseen circumstances and changes in trends and technology.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But today, to the best of my knowledge and from speaking to experts, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and everyday people who have to deal with these harms, we can legislate better with the amendments I have proposed and I hope that this House will accept them.

sections.label: Singapore online safety legislation
sections.summary: Singapore enacted POHA in 2014 and OCHA in 2023, and the MDDI GPC welcomes the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: At the legislative level, Singapore has taken progressive and steady steps to strengthen online safety.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: We enacted POHA in 2014, introduced the OCHA in 2023, and updated the Broadcasting Act and IMDA Codes of Practice to hold online platforms accountable for harmful content.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: In 2024, our Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Communications and Information, then chaired by Ms Tin Pei Ling with Members Ms Hany Soh, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Alex Yam and myself, filed a Motion titled "Building an Inclusive and Safe Digital Society." Together with more than 10 PAP MPs, we called for stronger safeguards against online harms such as cyberbullying and urged platforms to do more to protect users.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Hence, our MDDI GPC welcomes the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill, which builds on these foundations – from ground feedback, to action, to legislation and now continued advocacy in this House.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: This Bill strengthens the framework to ensure that victims of online harm can receive swift, effective and meaningful relief, while reinforcing the responsibilities of platforms and perpetrators alike.

sections.label: Definition of online harassment
sections.summary: The Bill defines online harassment as communicating material a reasonable person would consider threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent and likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: The Bill defines online harassment as the communication of material that a reasonable person would consider threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent, and likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress, or humiliation to the victim.

sections.label: USC user journey timeline
sections.summary: The question asks the expected time between a file being reported to OSC and OSC issuing a direction against the communicator, administrator and platform.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: In Handout 2, which was distributed earlier, on the USC User Journey, what is the expected time between "a file reported to OSC" to when the "OSC may issue direction against the communicator, administrator and platform?" In the earlier speech, Minister of State Rahayu shared that victims can file a report after reporting to the online platform where the harm is occurring.

sections.label: Closed group platform coverage
sections.summary: The question asks whether this will extend to closed groups or platforms such as WhatsApp, Telegram and WeChat.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Will this extend to closed group or platforms such as WhatsApp, Telegram and WeChat?

sections.label: Victim Support and Assurance Framework
sections.summary: The OSC could work with ministries, the Institute of Mental Health and social service providers to establish a Victim Support and Assurance Framework.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Working with the Ministry of Social and Family Development, Ministry of Education, the Institute of Mental Health and social service providers, the OSC could establish a Victim Support and Assurance Framework comprising a confidential helpline or online portal for guidance; access to counselling and trauma-support services; and collaboration to track and prevent recurring patterns of online abuse.

sections.label: Limiting appeals for timely relief
sections.summary: The speaker supports limiting appeals so that relief remains timely and accessible for those unable to sustain long or expensive proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Many may simply give up, unable to sustain long or expensive proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Hence, I support the approach of limiting appeals, to ensure that relief remains timely and accessible.

sections.label: Harassment definition, victim support, litigation culture
sections.summary: The speaker asks how online harassment is determined, stresses victim support coordinated by the OSC, and warns against excessive litigation culture.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: First, how do we determine online harassment and when will the remaining categories of online harms be implemented?

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Second, the importance of support for victims, including counselling assistance and guidance that can be coordinated by the OSC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: Third, ensuring this law does not bring about an excessive litigation culture, especially against the bigger firms that have the ability to intimidate victims with high legal costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: This law must ensure swift action and immediate relief to victims, so that justice can be achieved expeditiously.

sections.label: Clause 26 threshold for Commissioner directions
sections.summary: The speaker says clause 26's "reason to suspect" threshold is too low and proposes raising it to "reasonable grounds to believe".

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Clause 26 of the Bill sets the threshold at which the Commissioner may issue directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: We believe that threshold is too low, too low for the powers being granted. "Reason to suspect" is a subjective test, it permits actions based on intuition or preliminary information without requiring objective evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Our proposed amendment raises this to "reasonable grounds to believe".

sections.label: Fair comment on public interest
sections.summary: For clause 9, the amendment adds that communication is not harassment if it is fair comment on a matter of public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For clause 9 we add that communication is not harassment if it constitutes fair comment on a matter of public interest.

sections.label: Right of appeal to High Court
sections.summary: The amendment deletes two clauses and sub-clauses and inserts a new clause C establishing a right of appeal to the General Division of the High Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Our amendment deletes these two clauses and sub-clauses and inserts a new clause C, establishing a right of appeal to the General Division of the High Court.

sections.label: Doxxing definition in Clause 10
sections.summary: Clause 10 defines doxxing as publishing identity information likely intended to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Clause 10 defines doxxing as publishing identity information where a reasonable person would conclude was likely to have been intended to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

sections.label: Directions issued to platforms, appeal rights
sections.summary: Some directions go to communicators, others to platforms or administrators, and Clause 61(1)(e) lets the recipient appeal, not the communicator.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Some, including the stop communication and restraining directions, can be issued directly to the communicator, but others, such as Access Disabling, Account Restriction and Engagement Reduction Directions are issued to platforms or administrators.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Clause 61(1)(e) allows the recipient to appeal, but the communicator is not the recipient.

sections.label: Public agencies excluded from Part 5
sections.summary: Clause 4(2) states that public agencies cannot be given directions or orders under Part 5.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Clause 4(2) states that public agencies cannot be given directions or orders under Part 5.

sections.label: Class of Material Directions concerns
sections.summary: Clause 40, with clauses 30 and 33, is a Class of Material Direction, raising over-blocking concerns and questions on safeguards and remedies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Clause 40, along with clauses 30 and 33, is also a Class of Material Direction, so this raises related concerns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: These Class of Material Directions allow the Commissioner to issue Stop Communication Directions against entire categories of content, identified by specific identifiers, such as a username, a term, an online location.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If a victim's advocacy group reporting on an emerging category of online harms, as a warning to the community, posts about it, they may see that their material is swept up by mistake.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, on Class of Material Directions, I have two questions: what safeguards exist to prevent over-blocking and what remedy exists for users whose legitimate content is caught inadvertently by the directions?

sections.label: Part 5 directions and Commissioner discretion
sections.summary: Part 5 directions are quasi-judicial with no requirement to publish reasons, prompting a question on whether the Commissioner is bound by prior decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: There will be transparency and consistency through the common law process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But Part 5 directions, which are quasi-judicial in nature, there is no requirement for publishing reasons or directions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: There is no public record of how Commissioner interprets and applies the definitions of harm in Part 3 and other sections.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, I ask the Minister, will the Commissioner be bound by prior decisions that they have made, or will each case be decided on fresh discretion?

sections.label: Support for one-stop OSC centre
sections.summary: The speaker supports the OSC as a one-stop centre coordinating Government action and Takedown Directions, and urges clear takedown service standards.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: This "Groundhog Day" is what many victims face – harm that repeats and hope that fades.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: That is why I support the creation of the OSC, which is a one-stop centre to coordinate Government action and issue Takedown Directions across platforms.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: OSC can help victims in navigating and simplifying the reporting process, from navigating which protective online harms statutes to invoke – is it POHA, POFMA, the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act, OCHA, the Broadcasting Act – to ensuring that victims do not need to make multiple reports to multiple agencies and multiple social media platforms.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: I also urge that Ministry to set clear service standards for takedown speed.

sections.label: Reporting false or vexatious submissions
sections.summary: The speaker asks how the Commission will make reports simple to file while protecting against false or vexatious submissions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: Families deserve both a response and a resolution.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: I have several clarifications for the Minister: (a) how will the Commission ensure reports are simple to file, yet protected from false or vexatious submissions?

sections.label: Measuring reasonable measures by platforms
sections.summary: The speaker asks how "reasonable measures" will be measured and how OSC will assess compliance, especially for major platforms.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: And the Bill rightly requires platforms to "take reasonable measures" once notified of an online harm.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: But I would like to clarify on how this will be measured, what counts as "reasonable", and how OSC will assess compliance, particularly for major platforms with wide reach and significant influence.

sections.label: Partnerships for digital literacy and resilience
sections.summary: The speaker says Members, the OSC and the community must strengthen partnerships with Family Service Centres, schools, youth networks and grassroots organisations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: To complement this Bill, we, the Members of this House, the OSC, the community, must strengthen partnerships with our Family Service Centres, schools, youth networks and grassroots organisations, to build digital literacy, emotional resilience and first aid for the heart.

sections.label: Taking down harmful content quickly
sections.summary: The speaker states harmful content must be taken down as soon as possible because every hour of delay causes additional pain to affected families.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: When harmful content appears, it must be taken down as soon as possible.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: Every hour of delay causes additional pain to affected families.

sections.label: Harmful content affects every family
sections.summary: The speaker states harmful content affects every Singaporean family and that families and children are at the heart of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
sentences.text: Harmful content is not someone else's problem, but an issue that affect every Singaporean family. : Mr Speaker, at the heart of this Bill lies our families and children who form the soul of our communities.

sections.label: Adding two categories of online harm
sections.summary: The speaker notes the Bill's 13 categories of online harm and suggests adding content encouraging self-harm and suicide, and sexual grooming of children and vulnerable adults.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Bill currently includes 13 categories of online harm, including common online harassment, doxxing, online stalking, intimate image abuse and child sexual abuse material.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: We suggest including two additional categories of online harm, namely content that encourages self-harm and suicide and sexual grooming of children and vulnerable adults.

sections.label: Courts as final arbiter
sections.summary: The amendment proposes courts as final arbiter for appeals and requires the commission to submit annual reports to Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Our amendment proposal advocates for the courts to be the final arbiter for appeals, in order to improve the appeals mechanism and strengthen independent oversight.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Another suggestion is to enhance transparency and accountability mechanisms.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: We propose amendments requiring the commission to submit annual reports to Parliament.

sections.label: IMDA 2024 harmful content report
sections.summary: Ministers Teo and Tong cited IMDA's 2024 report finding platforms took five days or more to act on harmful content reports.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Ministers Teo and Tong referred to the IMDA's 2024 report, which found that platforms took an average of five days or more to act on user reports of harmful content that violated their own community guidelines.

sections.label: WP annual reports amendment
sections.summary: The WP tabled an amendment requiring the Commission to publish annual reports covering reports received, directions, turnaround times and online harm trends.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For this reason, the WP has tabled an amendment requiring the Commission to publish annual reports.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The report should contain: the number of reports received; quantity and types of directions and orders issued by the Commissioner; turnaround time for resolving reports; findings on risk assessments and trends relating to online harms.

sections.label: Sections 52 and 53 powers
sections.summary: Section 52 lets the Commissioner require providers to obtain end-user identity information; Section 53 allows disclosure to victims on reasonable suspicion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Section 52 allows the Commissioner to require an online service provider to obtain end-user identity information even if it is not already in the provider’s possession.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Section 53 allows the end-user identity information to be disclosed to victims for a prescribed purpose, based on reasonable suspicion that the end-user has engaged in harmful activity.

sections.label: Consistent application of definitions
sections.summary: The question asks what guidelines, training and objective criteria will ensure online harmful activity definitions are applied consistently, predictably and fairly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: What specific guidelines, training and objective criteria will be used to ensure the definitions of the various “online harmful activities” are applied consistently, predictably and fairly by the Commissioner?

sections.label: Verifying applicant intent and misuse
sections.summary: The question asks how the Commission will verify prescribed purpose intent, what conditions apply, and how it intervenes before criminal liability.

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Additionally, how will the Commission verify that applicants genuinely intend to use the information for a prescribed purpose?

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: What conditions will be imposed on the applicants who receive the identity information?

sentences.speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: How will the Commission intervene if it suspects that information was misused before criminal liability is established?

sections.label: Online harm victims access justice
sections.summary: It equips vulnerable individuals with tools to protect themselves and keeps laws relevant in the digital age, giving victims faster access to justice without new obstacles.

sentences.speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: It equips vulnerable individuals with tools to protect themselves and ensures that our laws stay relevant in the digital age.

sentences.speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: It allows victims of online harm to have faster access to justice and we must ensure that in doing so it does not introduce new obstacles that make it harder for victims to seek redress.

sections.label: Statutory civil wrong for victims
sections.summary: Recognising this as a statutory civil wrong offers victims a clear path to justice.

sentences.speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: By recognising this as a statutory civil wrong, the Bill offers victims a clear path to justice.

sections.label: Fast low-cost content correction
sections.summary: This mechanism offers a fast, low-cost way for victims to correct false or defamatory content, and asks whether it complements or substitutes Defamation Act remedies.

sentences.speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: This mechanism offers a fast, low-cost way for victims to correct false or defamatory content.

sentences.speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: However, will it complement or substitute existing remedies under the Defamation Act?

sections.label: OSC structure staffing expertise
sections.summary: As the OSC is to be established by next year, elaboration is sought on its structure, staffing and expertise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
sentences.text: As the OSC is to be established by next year, I seek elaboration on its structure, its staffing and its expertise.

sections.label: Minister directions to Commissioner
sections.summary: Clause 5(6) allows the Minister to give the Commissioner directions of a general or special character, not inconsistent with the Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, clause 5(6) of the Bill allows the Minister to give the Commissioner directions of a general or special character, not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act.

sections.label: Clause 22 victim ambit
sections.summary: Clarity is sought on clause 22, which states a victim of online harmful activity can be any citizen or Permanent Resident of Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In connection to this, I seek clarity on the ambit of clause 22, which states that a victim of online harmful activity can be anyone who is a citizen or Permanent Resident of Singapore.

sections.label: Commissioner powers and Meta compliance
sections.summary: Clause 52 lets the Commissioner obtain specified information about an end user, even outside Singapore, and asks for an update on Meta's compliance with an implementation directive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Clause 52 gives the Commissioner powers to obtain specified information about an end user and it does not matter if that end user is outside Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In this connection, can the Minister provide an update to the House on whether Meta has complied with the competent authorities' implementation directive to strengthen Facebook's measures against scams by 31 October this year as part of the OCHA.

sections.label: Commissioner and Appeal Committee duties
sections.summary: Clause 59(1)(d) requires the Commissioner to inform an applicant of a reconsidered decision within a reasonable time, while clause 64(5)(a) requires the Appeal Committee to state reasons for its appeal decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Clause 59(1)(d) requires the Commissioner to inform an applicant of the result of a reconsidered decision within a reasonable time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In contrast, on the matter of the Appeal Committee in clause 64(5)(a), the Committee is required to state the reasons for his decision in respect of the appeal.

sections.label: Tort of failing to respond
sections.summary: Clause 94 creates the tort of failing to respond reasonably to an online harm notice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Clause 94 creates the tort of failing to respond reasonably to an online harm notice.

sections.label: WP support and Sitting suspension
sections.summary: Subject to clarifications from the Ministers, the WP will support the Bill, and the Sitting is suspended to resume at 4.40 pm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the amendments in the name of He Ting Ru and subject to the clarifications from the Ministers, the WP will support the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: We have been in the Chamber for almost six hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: I suspend the Sitting and will assume the Chair at 4.40 pm.

sections.label: Victims' direct civil claims
sections.summary: Victims will have direct civil claims against perpetrators and against intermediaries or platform administrators who fail to act reasonably upon receiving a victim's notice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Victims will now have direct civil claims, not just against perpetrators, but also intermediaries or platform administrators who fail to act reasonably upon receiving a victim's notice.

sections.label: Right-of-Reply and Engagement Reduction Directions
sections.summary: The Bill introduces Right-of-Reply and Engagement Reduction Directions remedies, requiring platforms to push corrective replies and allowing the Commissioner to direct reduced engagement or amplification.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Second, the Bill introduces Right-of-Reply and Engagement Reduction Directions remedies that go beyond simple content removal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Platforms can now be required to push corrective replies to users who viewed the harmful content, ensuring that misinformation or defamation is countered in the same digital space.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Further, the Commissioner may direct platforms to reduce engagement or amplification; tackling not just content, but the algorithms that fuel virality and the harm.

sections.label: Judicial review and appeals limits
sections.summary: The passage states they remain subject to judicial review on conventional administrative law grounds, while the Bill limits appeals on the merits for swift, proportionate outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: They remain subject to judicial review on conventional administrative law grounds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: However, the Bill rightly limits appeals on the merits to ensure that outcomes are delivered swiftly and proportionately, especially where victims need urgent relief.

sections.label: Defence Guild SG founding
sections.summary: In 2021, the speaker and fellow lawyers established Defence Guild SG, a pro bono lawyer network defending victims of online and sexual harassment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In 2021, my fellow lawyers and I established Defence Guild SG, a pro bono lawyer network that defends victims of online harassment and sexual harassment.

sections.label: Defence Guild SG advisory services
sections.summary: The Defence Guild SG initiative, supported by Lawyers@M³, provides advisory services and legal help to those who may not qualify for formal legal aid.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: And that every victim has the right to legal protection that defends their dignity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: This Defence Guild SG initiative, supported by the Lawyers@M³ network, provides advisory services and legal help to those who may not qualify for formal legal aid.

sections.label: Bill enables immediate harassment relief
sections.summary: The passage states many victims remain silent because the judicial process takes time and money, and the Bill will enable victims to stop harassment immediately and avoid prolonged trauma.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Many victims choose to remain silent, because the judicial process takes time and money.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: But today, this Bill is not merely a piece of legislation, it will enable victims to stop harassment immediately, obtain justice quickly and most importantly, avoid prolonged trauma.

sections.label: OSC directions and civil recourse
sections.summary: The OSC is vested with authority to issue directions and orders to online service providers, communicators and administrators, and victims can turn to civil recourse and remedies.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: The OSC is vested with the authority to issue directions and orders to online service providers, communicators and administrators.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: Additionally, victims can turn to civil recourse and remedies for redress.

sections.label: IMDA 2024 Online Safety Assessment Report
sections.summary: IMDA's 2024 Online Safety Assessment Report found major platforms acted appropriately only on half of reported harmful content, often taking more than five days.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: IMDA’s 2024 Online Safety Assessment Report found that major platforms acted appropriately only on half of the reported harmful content, often taking more than five days.

sections.label: Powers to safeguard victims
sections.summary: Powers such as Stop Communication or Restraining Directions let victims take timely, decisive steps to safeguard themselves.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: Its powers, such as issuing Stop Communication or Restraining Directions, enable victims to take timely and decisive steps to safeguard themselves.

sections.label: Platform duty starts on report
sections.summary: The duty imposed on platforms starts only when the report is accurately and properly filed to the platform.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: The duty imposed on the platforms also only starts when the report is accurately and properly filed to the platform.

sections.label: Court proceedings and victim anonymity
sections.summary: The Bill envisages amended Rules of Court for redaction, private proceedings and identity orders, and suggests automatic redaction subject to judicial discretion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: In respect of court proceedings, the Bill envisages that the Rules of Court may be amended to empower the Court to order the redaction of identifying information, including parties' names, in court documents, to conduct proceedings in private, and to issue orders preventing the disclosure of parties’ or witnesses’ identities.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: I am concerned that in practice, however, victims may remain vulnerable and additional administrative steps may be required to secure their anonymity during the interim period before such orders are granted.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: I wish to suggest for the Minister's consideration whether a more victim-centric approach would be to introduce automatic redaction, subject to judicial discretion to lift such redaction where appropriate.

sections.label: Tort of online instigation
sections.summary: Clause 87 introduces a tort of online instigation of disproportionate harm offering civil recourse to victims and their associates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: Clause 87 of the Bill, which introduces the "tort of online instigation of disproportionate harm", which is designed to offer civil recourse to victims and their associates where public statements, made in response to a victim’s conduct, are likely to incite others to act in ways that could cause harm to the victim.

sections.label: Youths in drafting process
sections.summary: Youths who participated in drafting the legislation felt seen, heard, inspired and empowered, and the speaker is grateful their voices were heard.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: By participating in the drafting process of this legislation, our youths felt seen and heard, inspired and empowered.

sentences.speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
sentences.text: The youths had this to say: "Thank you for showing us that policy can be made with us, not just for us." I am grateful to the Government for allowing the youth voices to be heard on a Bill that affects matters close to their hearts.

sections.label: Rising doxxing and harassment cases
sections.summary: SHECARE@SCWO reports doxxing victims rose from 13 in 2023 to 32 in 2024, harassment and cyberbullying from 48 to 80, and Protection from Harassment Court applications rose to 631 in 2024.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
sentences.text: According to SHECARE@SCWO, victims of doxxing have risen from 13 in 2023 to 32 in 2024.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Harassment and cyberbullying cases rose from 48 to 80 in the same period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Applications to the Protection from Harassment Court have increased steadily: from 346 in 2021, to 520 in 2022, 526 in 2023, and 631 in 2024.

sections.label: Bill gives victims stronger recourse
sections.summary: The Bill gives victims stronger recourse and empowers the Commissioner to order platforms to remove or restrict content, require right-of-reply, or label harmful material.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
sentences.text: It tests the limits of what laws can do alone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
sentences.text: That is where this new Bill is crucial: it gives victims stronger recourse and empowers the Commissioner to put across platforms to remove or restrict content, require the right-of-reply, or label harmful material.

sections.label: Online harms spread and persist
sections.summary: Online harms spread instantaneously and beyond control, content can be duplicated and re-shared permanently, and victims struggle to have harmful content removed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: Unlike physical or verbal harassment, online harms spread instantaneously, exponentially and often beyond our immediate control.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: Content posted today can be duplicated, archived, indexed and re‑shared, leaving permanent scars on victims' reputations and livelihoods.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: It is easy for anyone to publish, but hard for victims, especially ordinary users, to have harmful content removed.

sections.label: Key features of amendment
sections.summary: The amendment's key features are a clearer definition of online harms, an Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety, and powers for speedy interventions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: The key features of this amendment are: firstly, a clearer definition of online harms; secondly, the establishment of an Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety; and thirdly, powers to enable speedy interventions when harms are detected.

sections.label: Welcome to finality in appeals
sections.summary: The Member welcomes the amendments' focus on finality in appeals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: Adding on, I wish to express my welcome to the amendments' focus on finality in appeals.

sections.label: Concerns about fair comment amendments
sections.summary: The Member asks whether fair comment would delay protection for public figures and says proposed amendments removing finality and changing suspicion to belief would drag out victims' exposure.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: Playing the devil's advocate, since the premise of this is to prevent the premature ending of the discussion of topics of public interests, possibly because of fear of political motivation, then does "fair comment" also mean that if a public figure happens to fall victim to baseless allegation, fake news or even being sexualised online, that this "fair comment" will prevent or delay protection and justice, just because the subject happens to be a public figure?

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: Also, the Member's proposed amendments suggest, or seems to suggest, the removal of finality to appeals and to switch from "reason to suspect" to "reason to believe" – these will drag out the process and extend a victim's exposure to harm.

sections.label: Key points of amendment
sections.summary: The amendment provides a clearer definition of online harm, establishes the OSC, and grants powers to intervene swiftly, addressing victims' problems of speed and uncertainty.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: The key points of this amendment includes: first, providing a clearer definition of online harm; second, establishing the OSC; and third, granting powers to intervene swiftly when harm is discovered.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
sentences.text: These measures can better address the problems victims frequently face, that is, speed and uncertainty.

sections.label: Reason to suspect versus believe
sections.summary: Changing the test from reason to suspect to reason to believe would take time and could expose already traumatised victims to further harm.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
sentences.text: Deputy Speaker, from "reason to suspect", it means that when the harm is first detected, that allows the agency or the authority to quickly step in and take measures to remove the harm.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
sentences.text: But to change it to "reason to believe" will mean that there must be sufficient grounds established to prove that there is indeed harm, and this process will take time.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
sentences.text: So, during this period of time, I am fearful or I am worried that this will cause the victim, who is already traumatised, to be exposed to the harm further.

sections.label: Reasonable grounds to believe
sections.summary: The thinking is that serious harm needing immediate address will meet the reasonable grounds to believe threshold upfront, allowing takedown.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
sentences.text: Our thinking behind is that if there is a serious harm needing immediate address, I believe the test of reasonable grounds to believe will meet the threshold upfront and therefore, allow a takedown of the content.

sections.label: Bill's purpose and scope
sections.summary: The Bill aims to give victims quick remedies through the Commissioner of Online Safety, addresses 13 harm classes and pervasiveness, and is not meant to regulate online content.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Its main purpose is to provide quick and effective remedies and relief to victims of online harms, through a straightforward and accessible reporting platform, the Commissioner of Online Safety.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: All 13 classes of online harms are addressed from the victim's perspective.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Two, it addresses the pervasiveness of the online harm, by factoring in considerations, such as the number, frequency, nature and circumstances of the online communication.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Third and importantly, this Bill should not be seen as an attempt to regulate online content.

sections.label: Australian Online Safety Act distinction
sections.summary: The Australian Online Safety Act 2021 distinguishes between cyberbullying for children and cyber-abuse for adults.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: The Australian Online Safety Act 2021, for instance, draws a distinction between cyberbullying for children and cyber-abuse for adults.

sections.label: Gamers bullied survey results
sections.summary: 17% of gamers aged 13 to 18 felt bullied in video games, and 48% of those took no action.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: The results are as follows: 17% or almost one in five gamers aged 13 to 18 felt that they have been bullied in video games by other players.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Out of the 17% who felt bullied, nearly half or 48% did not take any action at all.

sections.label: UCLA cyberbullying survey findings
sections.summary: In a UCLA survey of 1,400 youths aged 12 to 17, 90% did not tell an adult about the cyberbullying incident.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: In another survey conducted by researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) on how 1,400 youths aged 12 to 17 deal with cyberbullying, 90% of the respondents reported that they did not tell an adult about the incident.

sections.label: Online safety multi-pronged approach
sections.summary: A multi-pronged approach led by the Commissioner for Online Safety would involve parents, educators, social workers, psychologists and counsellors, and the Member asks about plans and support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: To achieve this, it will likely entail a multi-pronged approach led by the Commissioner for Online Safety, involving the entire ecosystem that supports our children and youths from parents, educators, social workers, child psychologists and student guidance counsellors to name a few.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: In this context, I would ask the Minister of the Government’s views and plans to address the complexities and nuances of online harms suffered by children or youths in the digital world and, if there are plans to augment the Office of the Commissioner for Online Safety with the necessary support, such as a professionally trained team of experts to address these issues.

sections.label: Fair comment carve-out for online harassment
sections.summary: The Member argues online harassment could be broadly defined with an express carve-out for fair comments, as section 19 sets a definition then a carve-out.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
sentences.text: The words complained of are "comments", "though they may consist of or include inferences of facts", "the comment is a matter of public interest, "the comment is based on facts", and finally "the comment is one of which a fair-minded person can honestly make on the facts proved".

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
sentences.text: I do not intend to belabour the court with an extended discussion on the legalese here.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
sentences.text: So, the crux of my point is that section 19, also a definition of online harm, has the structure of first setting out a definition before proceeding to have a carve-out.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
sentences.text: So, I do not see why we do not – we cannot treat other definitions and other harms the same way, where we are proposing that you have a broad definition of what online harassment could be, and we explicitly and expressly carve out fair comments, so that there is clarity for everyone who is reading the legislation.

sections.label: Clause 9 online harassment definition
sections.summary: The Member says that based on the definition, no online communication could be caught under clause 9 on online harassment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo
sentences.text: Based on that definition, I cannot imagine that there could be any online communication that would be caught under the definition of clause 9 – online harassment – and that is my point.

sections.label: Single front door for victims
sections.summary: For the first time, victims have a single front door and a clear pathway to redress.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: For the first time, victims have a single front door and a clear pathway to redress.

sections.label: Powers for online safety commissioner
